questions.q: A firm's Revaluation Account shows a credit total of ₹1,20,000 and debit total of ₹75,000. The old profit sharing ratio is 3:2. What amount will be credited to each old partner's Capital Account for revaluation profit, and why is it distributed in the old ratio rather than the new ratio?
questions.a: Revaluation profit = ₹1,20,000 - ₹75,000 = ₹45,000. Partner A (3/5) gets ₹27,000 credit; Partner B (2/5) gets ₹18,000 credit. Revaluation profit/loss belongs to the period BEFORE admission, so it's distributed to old partners in their OLD profit sharing ratio. The new partner was not part of the firm when the revaluation gain/loss arose. WRONG ANSWER REVEALS: If a student distributes in new ratio, they confuse revaluation (pre-admission event) with goodwill/reserves (which may involve new partner's sacrifice/gain). If they forget to calculate net profit first, they lack basic ledger balancing skill.

questions.q: In the Capital Account of an old partner, you see these credit entries: Opening Balance ₹2,00,000; General Reserve ₹30,000; Revaluation Profit ₹15,000; Goodwill (premium brought by new partner) ₹40,000. Debit entries: Drawings ₹10,000; Goodwill written off (existing) ₹20,000. The new partner brings ₹50,000 capital for 1/5th share. Calculate the old partner's closing capital balance. Then explain: why is existing goodwill written off in OLD ratio but new goodwill premium credited in SACRIFICING ratio?
questions.a: Closing Capital = 2,00,000 + 30,000 + 15,000 + 40,000 - 10,000 - 20,000 = ₹2,55,000. Existing goodwill appears in books at historical value — it belongs to old partners in their OLD ratio, so written off in old ratio. New goodwill premium is brought by new partner for the share SACRIFICED by old partners, so credited in SACRIFICING ratio. WRONG ANSWER REVEALS: If student uses new ratio for existing goodwill write-off, they don't understand that existing goodwill was created by old partners' past efforts. If they use old ratio for new goodwill premium, they confuse sacrifice (giving up share) with entitlement (past ownership).

questions.q: A and B share profits 3:2. They admit C for 1/4th share. C brings ₹80,000 capital and ₹20,000 goodwill premium. Goodwill premium is distributed in sacrificing ratio 3:2. After all adjustments, A's capital = ₹2,10,000, B's capital = ₹1,40,000. The firm decides total capital should be ₹5,00,000 in new profit sharing ratio. Calculate how much cash A and B must bring/withdraw. Show the journal entries.
questions.a: New ratio: A = 3/4 × 3/4 = 9/16? Wait — C gets 1/4, remaining 3/4 shared by A,B in 3:2 → A = 3/5 × 3/4 = 9/20, B = 2/5 × 3/4 = 6/20, C = 5/20. Total capital ₹5,00,000 → A's new capital = 9/20 × 5,00,000 = ₹2,25,000 (bring ₹15,000), B's = 6/20 × 5,00,000 = ₹1,50,000 (bring ₹10,000), C's = 5/20 × 5,00,000 = ₹1,25,000 (already brought ₹80,000? Wait — C brought ₹80,000 capital, so C needs to bring ₹45,000 more). Journal: Bank Dr. 15,000 → A's Capital; Bank Dr. 10,000 → B's Capital; Bank Dr. 45,000 → C's Capital. WRONG ANSWER REVEALS: If student calculates new ratio incorrectly (e.g., 3:2:1), they haven't mastered node 02_001. If they forget C's capital adjustment, they treat capital proportion adjustment as only for old partners. If they debit capital for bringing cash, they reverse debit/credit rule.

questions.q: Compare the Revaluation Account format for admission vs. retirement. In admission, revaluation profit is credited to OLD partners in OLD ratio. In retirement, revaluation profit is credited to ALL partners (including retiring) in OLD ratio. Why is the retiring partner included but the new partner excluded? What happens if revaluation shows a LOSS instead of profit?
questions.a: Retiring partner is included because they were a partner DURING the period when the revaluation gain/loss arose — they bear the economic consequence. New partner is excluded because they join AFTER the revaluation date. If revaluation shows a LOSS: Revaluation Account Dr. → Old Partners' Capital Accounts Cr. (in old ratio) for admission; Revaluation Account Dr. → All Partners' Capital Accounts Cr. (in old ratio) for retirement. WRONG ANSWER REVEALS: If student says retiring partner excluded, they think retirement severs all ties immediately. If they say new partner included in admission, they confuse admission date with revaluation date. If they reverse debit/credit for loss, they don't understand nominal account rules.

questions.q: Evaluate this statement: "When preparing the post-admission Balance Sheet, the new partner's capital is always shown at the amount they brought in cash." Provide a counterexample where this is false, and explain the correct principle for determining the new partner's capital in the Balance Sheet.
questions.a: Statement is FALSE. Counterexample: New partner brings ₹1,00,000 cash for 1/5th share. Total capital of firm based on this = ₹5,00,000. Old partners' adjusted capitals = ₹3,50,000 + ₹1,00,000 = ₹4,50,000. To make capitals proportionate, new partner's capital should be ₹1,00,000 (already correct) — but if old partners' capitals after adjustments are ₹4,20,000, total capital = ₹5,20,000, new partner's share = 1/5 × 5,20,000 = ₹1,04,000. New partner must bring additional ₹4,000. Correct principle: New partner's capital in Balance Sheet = their proportionate share of total firm capital (sum of all partners' adjusted capitals + new partner's contribution) in the NEW profit sharing ratio. WRONG ANSWER REVEALS: Student thinks capital account = cash brought only, ignoring proportionate capital adjustment (node 02_008) and the fact that capital accounts reflect ownership claim, not just cash inflow.

questions.q: Create a mini-case: Design an admission scenario with 3 old partners (ratio 4:3:2), 1 new partner, where: (a) Revaluation shows profit, (b) Existing goodwill written off, (c) New goodwill premium brought, (d) General Reserve distributed, (e) Capitals made proportionate. Provide the pre-admission Balance Sheet and admission terms. Then write the Revaluation Account, all Capital Accounts, and post-admission Balance Sheet. Your case must require at least 5 journal entries from node 02_009.
questions.a: Expected: A complete worked case with Balance Sheet (assets/liabilities), admission terms (new ratio, goodwill value, revaluation items, reserve amount, capital proportion terms), Revaluation Account with 3+ items, 4 Capital Accounts (3 old + 1 new) with all adjustments, and Balance Sheet with correct totals. Good answer shows: proper T-account format, correct distribution ratios (old for revaluation/reserve/existing goodwill, sacrificing for new goodwill), capital proportion adjustment with cash bring/withdraw, and Balance Sheet balancing. POOR ANSWER REVEALS: If student omits existing goodwill write-off, they miss node 02_005/02_009. If they use new ratio for reserve distribution, they confuse pre-admission vs post-admission events. If Balance Sheet doesn't balance, they have arithmetic errors or missed postings.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Preparation of Revaluation Account, Partners' Capital Accounts, and Balance Sheet after Admission is the systematic process of recording the effects of asset/liability revaluation, goodwill adjustment, accumulated profit/loss distribution, and capital ______ in ledger accounts to reflect the reconstituted partnership's financial position immediately after a new partner is admitted.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you're the accountant for a ______ firm where a new partner is joining tomorrow.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to independently prepare a complete Revaluation Account, Partners' Capital Accounts (old and new partners), and the post-admission Balance Sheet from a given pre-admission Balance Sheet and admission terms, showing all adjustments in correct format with proper narration.
